To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CT scans of the brain are often requested in the acute setting for non-head trauma in children, and there is a low referral threshold for CT scans in children with suspected encephalitis/meningitis.

CT brain scan has low clinical referral threshold in children with suspected meningitis, but has a poor positive predictive values in the diagnosis of meningococcal meningitis and raised intracellular pressure.

there is no direct correlation of the findings of CT scan with signs of raised ICP and there is a low positive predictive value of the CT findings in the diagnoses of meningoencecephalitis and raised ICP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of CT scans in the diagnosis of meningococcal disease.
the clinical indications of CT brain imaging in pediatric non-traumatic patients.
the use of computed tomography (brain) in the management of pediatric patients in the acute setting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of CT brain imaging should be restricted to those with clinical signs and symptoms suggestive of raised intracerebral pressure and/or intracranial pathology.
CT scan of the brain in children with non-head injuries has limited value in the diagnosis of meningoencephalitis and raised ICP.
CT brain scan has a low predictive value in the diagnosis of raised intracerebral pressure and encephalitis in children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of CT scan in the acute setting is not without its limitations, and the use of MRI in certain clinical scenarios may be a more valuable tool.
CT scan of the brain is valuable in the management of children with suspected menigoencephalitis but not in those with non-traumatic intracranial pathology.
the indications for CT brain imaging were not always appropriate and the scan request was not always in line with the British Society of Paediatric Radiology (BSR) guidelines.
The main takeaway from our work is that

CT scans should be performed in children with suspected intracerebral pathology in the appropriate clinical settings and the risk of ionizing radiation should not be ignored.
Keywords:
the CT scan is a valuable tool in the management of children presenting with neurological complaints.
CT brain scan has a limited role in the diagnosis and management of meningoencecephalitis and raised ICP in children and should not be used indiscriminately.
